subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Nazia, and I once spent an entire evening hurt by one word. My group-project partner Bidisha had messaged me, "Fine." That was all. I'd asked if she could send her slides by Thursday, and she wrote "Fine." No emoji, no exclamation, no "sure!" like she usually sent. I read it as anger. I stared at the screen for an hour, drafting a cold reply, then deleting it. Finally I called her instead. She picked up on the first ring, sounding out of breath. "Sorry, I was on the bus in the rain, I could only type one word! Slides tomorrow, promise." I sat there feeling silly and relieved. Now, when a message sounds cold, I try to ask before I decide it is.

qa.q: What single word did Bidisha send?
What did Nazia feel when she read the word, and what was the actual reason for its brevity?
qa.a: Nazia felt hurt, reading it as anger, but Bidisha was simply on a rainy bus and could type only one word.

qa.q: What could Nazia do the next time a message seems cold?
qa.a: Nazia could ask a quick clarifying question or call, instead of guessing the mood from a short text.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Nazia called?
qa.a: Bidisha was probably surprised and apologetic, as she was out of breath and hadn't realised how her one word sounded.

grounding: Nazia misreads a rushed, brief text as anger and checks by calling.

subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Akash came in upset about an email from his lab supervisor, Jahnavi, that read only: "Send me the data. Now." He had taken it as anger and was rehearsing what to say to withdraw from the project. I asked what else could explain the message. He listed a few: she might be rushed, or on her phone, or in a meeting. We agreed the email itself did not tell us her tone. I suggested he reply briefly and ask, "Do you need the raw file or the summary, and by when?" That gives her something easy to answer. He did, and she answered within a minute: raw file, before her flight. Akash relaxed and said he should have checked first. I will note that his worry was understandable.

qa.a: It said, "Send me the data. Now."

qa.q: What did Akash believe about the email at first, and what did the counsellor help him see?
qa.a: He believed Jahnavi was angry, and the counsellor helped him see that the short wording could also mean she was rushed or busy.

qa.q: What could Akash do in future when a message seems curt?
qa.a: He could reply with a short, specific question, or call, to check what the sender needs instead of assuming anger.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have seen her own message?
qa.a: She probably wrote it quickly because she was rushing to catch a flight, and may not have realised it could sound harsh.

grounding: A counsellor helps Akash see that a curt email may simply be rushed and to check before assuming anger.
